title: How To Use ‘The Power Of One’ Strategy To Improve Behavior mprove-behavior/
author: Michael Linsin
summary: Linsin introduces the 'power of one' strategy, a proactive technique for any routine or task a class needs to perform, from lining up to turning in work. The method has five steps: pause after giving directions, choose one student to model the task alone while classmates watch, let that student perform it without commentary, allow brief questions, and then have the whole class perform it together on a simple signal. He explains that the technique works because of the gentle social pressure on the chosen student to perform correctly, and because peer modeling motivates the rest of the class to match that standard without a hovering, micromanaging teacher. Its only real limitation is time, since it works best for tasks that take less than a couple of minutes. Linsin closes by arguing that this kind of simple, well-executed technique tends to have an outsized impact on classroom management.
points: Follow five sequential steps—pause, choose one student, let them perform silently, allow brief questions, then signal the whole class to perform.
Use the strategy for any short routine or task, from lining up for recess to turning in work or gathering materials.
The chosen student's performance creates positive social pressure and gives the rest of the class a peer model to imitate.
Offer a small gesture of praise to the modeling student rather than narrating or interrupting the demonstration.
Reserve the strategy for tasks that take less than a couple of minutes; break longer routines into smaller chunks modeled by different students.
quotes: You’re going to love this classroom management strategy. So much so that you may end up using it every day—maybe several times a day.

A pause creates anticipation, drawing more attention to you and interest in whatever comes next. It also gives you a moment to glance around the room and confirm that your students are attentive and ready to begin.
Don’t say a word while the chosen student is performing the task. Stand at a distance and watch to make sure it is done correctly.
There is soft pressure on the chosen student. And as long as you’re clear with your instructions, he or she will be determined to perform the task exactly as taught.
This form of modeling is made all the more effective because a student is doing the modeling–and without a hovering, play-by-play calling, micromanaging teacher.
The longer I teach the more I’m convinced that simple things done well have the greatest impact on classroom management.
